source_text: Post haec, omnem illum contextum de Abraham et Sara, qui emortuis iam corporibus filium pro munere acceperunt, quorum exemplum quantum veritati suffragetur, non solum sapiens, sed etiam mediocris lector intellegit, sic praeteriit, ut diceret contra se non multum valere. A qua impudentia vel illa eum debuit revocare sententia, quae ita constructa est: Et ut breviter, inquio, disputationis huius summa claudatur; si per concupiscentiam redditus est quem Deus promisit, bona sine dubio quae absolvit Dei fidem; si sine concupiscentia, noxia non potest esse progenito; quae nec cum conciperetur, nec cum pareretur, interfuit.
pass_a_gloss: After these things, that whole context about Abraham and Sarah, who with bodies already dead received a son as a gift, whose example how much it suffrages for truth not only a wise but even a middling reader understands, he so passed over that he said it does not avail much against him. From which shamelessness even that sentence ought to have called him back, which was so constructed: And that briefly, I say, the sum of this disputation may be closed; if through desire he was restored whom God promised, good without doubt are those things which loosed God's faith; if without desire, what was present neither when he was conceived nor when he was born cannot be harmful to the one begotten.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: After this he passed over the whole continuous discussion of Abraham and Sarah, who received a son as a gift when their bodies were already as good as dead (Romans 4:19; Genesis 21:1–2). Even an ordinary reader, not only a wise one, understands how strongly their example supports the truth. He passed it over by saying it carried little weight against him. At least this statement, framed as follows, should have recalled him from such shamelessness: ‘To bring this argument’s main point to a brief conclusion: if the child whom God promised was given through sexual desire, then what fulfilled God’s pledge was undoubtedly good. If he was given without sexual desire, desire cannot harm the offspring, since it was present neither when he was conceived nor when he was born.’

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
